title: Spreadsheet Data Analysis: Formulas, Pivot Tables and Charts
subtitle: Clean, look up, summarise and chart data in Excel, Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc, then build what-if models with validation, scenario tables and Goal Seek.
outcomes: Set data up as a tidy table, import CSV files and write formulas with relative, absolute and mixed references
Clean text, dates and numbers stored as text, and find duplicates and gaps with formulas and checks
Look up values with XLOOKUP, INDEX/MATCH and VLOOKUP, and diagnose lookups that fail
Summarise data with SUMIFS, COUNTIFS and AVERAGEIFS, pivot tables and charts
Validate input and build what-if models with scenario tables and Goal Seek
prerequisites: Basic computer skills: opening files, typing, copying and pasting. You need one spreadsheet app: Microsoft Excel (XLOOKUP needs Microsoft 365 or Excel 2021 or later), Google Sheets (free, in a browser) or LibreOffice Calc (free; XLOOKUP needs 24.8 or later). The labs give alternatives where the apps differ, and the data comes with them.
description:
Spreadsheets are where most of the world's data analysis happens, and a few well-chosen techniques turn them from a grid of numbers into a reliable analysis tool. This course teaches them in Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets and LibreOffice Calc side by side, noting where the three differ, through a year of (made-up) sales from Morning Loaf, a bakery with three branches. You'll start by setting data up as a tidy table, importing CSV files safely and writing formulas whose relative, absolute and mixed references behave when they're copied. Then you'll clean a messy export of online orders: stray spaces, inconsistent capitals, dates stored as digits, amounts stored as text and duplicate rows.

Next come lookups, with XLOOKUP, and INDEX/MATCH and VLOOKUP for older versions, including approximate matches for bands and the reasons lookups fail. You'll summarise the year with SUMIFS, COUNTIFS and AVERAGEIFS, building a branch-by-month grid from one formula, check it against a pivot table and chart the result. Finally you'll protect input with data validation and build a what-if model of a price change, with a scenario table and Goal Seek. Every lab adds to one workbook and has exact results to check, worked out from the same data, and the capstone is a full analysis for the bakery's owners. Data Storytelling and Dashboard Design builds on it, and Data Analysis with Python and pandas is the next step when data outgrows a spreadsheet.

modules.title: Formulas and references
modules.summary: Set data up as a tidy table, import a CSV file into Excel, Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc, and write formulas whose references behave when they're copied.

lessons.title: Setting up data for analysis
objectives: Lay data out as a tidy table that formulas, filters and pivot tables can use
Import a CSV file into Excel, Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc
Freeze the header row and filter the data
key_points: Keep data as one table per sheet: one header row, one record per row, one kind of value per column, and no blank rows, merged cells or subtotals inside it; formulas, filters and pivot tables all rely on that shape.
Keep the raw data on its own sheet and do the analysis on other sheets, so the original records are never overwritten and every result can be traced back to them.

A CSV file holds only text: on import, each app guesses which values are numbers and dates using your locale, so check that numbers sit on the right of their cells (where numbers go by default) and that dates were recognised before trusting any total.

Freeze the header row so column names stay in view while you scroll (the View menu's Freeze options in all three apps), and add filters to sort and filter each column (Data > Filter in Excel, Data > Create a filter in Google Sheets, Data > AutoFilter in LibreOffice Calc).
Give columns short, clear names, such as unit_price, and record units where everyone will see them, such as a note that prices are in pounds.

walkthrough.tool: Excel, Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc
walkthrough.title: Import a CSV file and check it

steps.do: Excel: choose Data > From Text/CSV, pick sales_2025.csv, check the preview (comma as the delimiter, dates in the date column), then choose Load.
steps.see: The data opens on a new sheet as a formatted table.

steps.do: Google Sheets: in a new spreadsheet, choose File > Import > Upload and pick the file; choose Replace spreadsheet (or Insert new sheet), leave the separator on Detect automatically and Convert text to numbers, dates and formulas ticked, then Import data.
LibreOffice Calc: choose File > Open and pick the file; in the Text Import dialog, tick Comma as the separator and tick Detect special numbers, so dates are recognised, then OK.
Check the shape: 368 rows of data under one header row, and the last row's sale_id is S0368.
steps.see: In every app, the row numbers show 369 rows including the header.

steps.do: Check the types: quantities and prices sit on the right of their cells, and clicking a date shows it as a date, not text, in the formula bar.
Rename the sheet Sales (right-click its tab), then freeze the first row with the View menu's Freeze options and turn on the filter buttons.

lessons.title: Formulas, functions and errors
objectives: Write formulas with operators and functions
Choose between results with IF
Recognise and fix the common error values
key_points: A formula starts with = and recalculates when its inputs change: + - * / and ^ do arithmetic, & joins text, and all three apps follow the usual order (brackets, then powers, then * and /, then + and -).
SUM, AVERAGE, MIN and MAX summarise a range such as H2:H369 or a whole column such as H:H; COUNT counts cells holding numbers, while COUNTA counts every cell that isn't empty, header included.
IF(test, value_if_true, value_if_false) chooses between results, as in =IF(G2="Cash", 0, H2*0.02); AND and OR combine tests, and comparisons of text ignore case.

Error values point to the problem: #DIV/0! is division by zero, #N/A means a lookup found nothing, #VALUE! a wrong type (such as text in arithmetic), #REF! a reference to deleted cells and #NAME? a misspelt or unsupported function.
ROUND(value, 2) changes the stored value, while number formatting only changes how it's displayed; round when the rounded amount is what really happens, such as a fee charged in whole pence.
Show the formulas instead of their results to check a sheet: Formulas > Show Formulas in Excel, View > Show > Formulas in Google Sheets and View > Show Formula in LibreOffice Calc.

lessons.title: Relative, absolute and mixed references
objectives: Explain what happens to references when a formula is copied
Fix the row, the column or both with $
Refer to cells on other sheets and to named ranges
key_points: References are relative by default: copying =E2*F2 down one row gives =E3*F3, which is what a calculation repeated on every row needs.

A $ fixes what follows it: $B$1 always points at B1, $B1 fixes only the column and B$1 only the row; F4 cycles through the forms in Excel for Windows and Google Sheets (Cmd+T in Excel for Mac), and Shift+F4 does it in LibreOffice Calc.

Use an absolute reference for one input that many formulas share, such as a fee rate in Totals!$B$1, so it's changed in one place; without the $, copied formulas point at empty cells and quietly return 0.
Mixed references let one formula fill a grid: with $A2 (labels down column A) and B$1 (headings across row 1), the formula picks up the right label and heading wherever it's copied.

A reference to another sheet is written Totals!B1 in Excel and Google Sheets ('Sheet name'!B1 when the name has spaces) and $Totals.B1 in LibreOffice Calc; clicking the cell while typing a formula writes the right form for you.

A named range, such as fee_rate for Totals!$B$1, makes formulas easier to read (=H2*fee_rate) and is absolute automatically: Formulas > Define Name in Excel, Data > Named ranges in Google Sheets, Sheet > Named Ranges and Expressions > Define in LibreOffice Calc.

One workbook for the whole course: every later lab adds sheets to it

hints: If SUM gives 0 or a smaller total, some numbers came in as text (they sit on the left of the cell): re-import, or convert them with VALUE.
Fees of 0 on every row mean the rate reference is wrong or empty: check that it points at Totals!$B$1.
Your app may use semicolons between a function's arguments, as in =IF(G2="Cash";0;...), depending on your language settings; LibreOffice Calc's help writes formulas that way too.
If your results show 4.017,50, your settings use a comma as the decimal separator; that's the same number.

modules.title: Cleaning text and dates
modules.summary: Fix the mess exports bring: stray spaces and inconsistent capitals, dates stored as digits, numbers stored as text, duplicates and gaps, using formulas in helper columns and checks that count problems.

lessons.title: Cleaning text
objectives: Clean text with TRIM, CLEAN, PROPER, UPPER and LOWER
Extract and replace parts of text
Turn cleaned formulas into values
key_points: TRIM removes spaces at the start and end of text and shrinks runs of spaces inside it to one, CLEAN removes non-printing characters, and PROPER, UPPER and LOWER fix the capitals: =PROPER(TRIM(C2)) turns '  YARA  NASSER ' into 'Yara Nasser'.

LEFT, RIGHT and MID take characters from the start, end or middle of text, LEN counts them, and FIND (case-sensitive) and SEARCH (not) give a character's position, so =LEFT(A2, FIND(" ", A2) - 1) takes the first word.
SUBSTITUTE(text, old, new) replaces every occurrence of some text, as in =SUBSTITUTE(E2, " GBP", "") to strip a currency code; & joins text, and TEXTJOIN joins a whole range with a separator.
A space copied from a web page may be a non-breaking space, CHAR(160), which TRIM leaves alone: replace it first, as in =TRIM(SUBSTITUTE(A2, CHAR(160), " ")).

Clean in helper columns beside the original, check the results, then replace the formulas with their values (Paste Special > Values in Excel and LibreOffice Calc, Edit > Paste special > Values only in Google Sheets) before deleting the original column.
Text to Columns splits one column into several at a delimiter such as a comma: Data > Text to Columns in Excel and LibreOffice Calc, Data > Split text to columns in Google Sheets.

lessons.title: Dates and numbers stored as text
objectives: Explain how spreadsheets store dates and times
Build dates from text and take them apart
Convert numbers stored as text
key_points: A date is stored as a serial number, a count of days, with the time of day as a fraction; Excel, Google Sheets and LibreOffice Calc give the same serial numbers for dates from March 1900 on, so =B3-B2 gives the days between two dates.
DATE(year, month, day) builds a date from numbers; YEAR, MONTH, DAY and WEEKDAY(date, 2) (Monday 1 to Sunday 7) take one apart, and EOMONTH(date, 0) gives the last day of its month.

Exports often hold dates as digits or text, such as 20250314: =DATE(LEFT(B2, 4), MID(B2, 5, 2), RIGHT(B2, 2)) builds a real date in any locale, while DATEVALUE reads a text date using the locale's order of day and month.

03/04/2025 is 3 April in the UK and 4 March in the US, so an import can silently swap day and month: check a few dates whose day is above 12, and prefer the ISO form, 2025-03-04, which every app reads the same way.

Numbers stored as text sit on the left of their cells and SUM skips them: VALUE converts them, as in =VALUE(SUBSTITUTE(E2, " GBP", "")); in Excel and LibreOffice Calc, NUMBERVALUE(text, ".") reads a decimal point the same way whatever the locale.
TEXT(date, "yyyy-mm") turns a date into a label such as 2025-03; its format codes depend on the language of Excel and LibreOffice, such as "JJJJ" for the year in German.

lessons.title: Duplicates, blanks and quality checks
objectives: Find and remove duplicate records
Highlight duplicates and blanks with conditional formatting
Write checks that count the problems left
key_points: =COUNTIF($A$2:A2, A2) > 1 is TRUE from a value's second appearance on, because the range grows as the formula is copied down: it flags duplicates while keeping each first copy.

Data > Remove Duplicates (Excel) and Data > Data cleanup > Remove duplicates (Google Sheets) delete repeated rows; in LibreOffice Calc, Data > More Filters > Standard Filter with No duplications copies the unique rows elsewhere. Decide first which columns define a duplicate.

Conditional formatting shows problems at a glance: highlight duplicates (Excel's Highlight Cells Rules > Duplicate Values, Calc's 'is duplicate' condition, or a custom formula with COUNTIF in Google Sheets) and blank cells, which usually mean missing rather than zero.
Check the cleaning with formulas that count problems, such as =COUNTBLANK(F2:F66) for missing dates and =SUMPRODUCT(--ISTEXT(I2:I66)) for amounts still stored as text: the target is zero.
Count distinct values with =SUMPRODUCT(1/COUNTIF(G2:G66, G2:G66)), which works everywhere, or =COUNTA(UNIQUE(G2:G66)) in Microsoft 365, Excel 2021, Google Sheets and LibreOffice Calc 24.8 or later.
Keep a log of each cleaning step, such as '5 duplicate rows removed', so anyone can see what changed between the export and your results.

lab.title: Clean a messy order export
lab.tool: Excel, Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc
lab.goal: Clean the bakery's export of online pre-orders: build real dates from digits, tidy names and items, turn amounts stored as text into numbers, flag duplicate rows, and count what's left with checks.

Type these headings in F1:J1: date, customer_clean, item_clean, amount_value, duplicate.

steps.do: In J2, flag repeats of an order reference, keeping the first copy.
Select F2:J2 and fill down to row 66.
Build a checks block: labels in L2:L7 and formulas in M2:M7.
steps.code:
L2 Duplicate rows              M2 =COUNTIF(J2:J66,"Duplicate")
L3 Unique orders               M3 =COUNTA(A2:A66)-M2
L4 Value of unique orders      M4 =SUMIFS(I2:I66,J2:J66,"<>Duplicate")
L5 Unique orders in March      M5 =COUNTIFS(F2:F66,">="&DATE(2025,3,1),F2:F66,"<="&DATE(2025,3,31),J2:J66,"<>Duplicate")
L6 Distinct customers          M6 =SUMPRODUCT(1/COUNTIF(G2:G66,G2:G66))
L7 Celebration cakes ordered   M7 =COUNTIFS(H2:H66,"Celebration Cake",J2:J66,"<>Duplicate")
steps.see: 5, 60, 1,100.00 (formatted with two decimals), 11, 25 and 22.

steps.do: Highlight the duplicates with conditional formatting on column A, then add a note on the sheet logging what you cleaned and what you found.

#VALUE! in I2 usually means VALUE couldn't read 12.50 because your locale expects a decimal comma: use the NUMBERVALUE version.

modules.title: Lookups
modules.summary: Bring information from one table into another with XLOOKUP, or INDEX/MATCH and VLOOKUP where XLOOKUP isn't available, use approximate matches for bands, and find out why lookups fail.

lessons.title: XLOOKUP
objectives: Look up values with XLOOKUP
Handle missing matches with if_not_found
Use approximate matches for bands and tiers
key_points: =XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found], [match_mode], [search_mode]) finds a value in one range and returns what's in the same position of another, as in =XLOOKUP(D2, Products!$A$2:$A$17, Products!$C$2:$C$17).
XLOOKUP matches exactly by default and returns #N/A when nothing matches; the fourth argument replaces that, such as "Not found", which is clearer than a blank that looks like real data.

match_mode -1 returns the exact match or the next smaller value, so a table of thresholds (1 Single, 4 Small batch, 10 Large order) puts every quantity in its band; 1 returns the next larger, and 2 allows wildcards such as "BR*".
search_mode -1 searches from the last row up, returning the last match, such as a customer's most recent order; the default, 1, returns the first.
XLOOKUP works in Microsoft 365, Excel 2021 and later, Google Sheets and LibreOffice Calc 24.8 and later; older versions show #NAME?, so use INDEX and MATCH in files that must work everywhere.
Lock the lookup ranges with $ (or use named ranges) before filling a lookup down, so every row searches the same table.

lessons.title: INDEX/MATCH and VLOOKUP
objectives: Write INDEX/MATCH lookups that work in every spreadsheet
Use VLOOKUP safely and know its limits
Look up a value by row and column at once
key_points: MATCH(value, range, 0) gives the position of the first exact match and INDEX(range, position) the item at a position; together, =INDEX(Products!$C$2:$C$17, MATCH(D2, Products!$A$2:$A$17, 0)) works like XLOOKUP in every version of every app.

MATCH's last argument matters: 0 means exact, while 1, used when it's left out, means the largest value less than or equal to the lookup value in a range sorted in ascending order, which gives wrong answers on unsorted data without any error.

VLOOKUP(value, table, column_number, FALSE) searches the first column of a table and returns the given column; it can't look to the left, and its column number doesn't change when columns are inserted, so it can break silently.

VLOOKUP's last argument defaults to TRUE, an approximate match on sorted data: always write FALSE for an exact match, and use TRUE deliberately for bands, as in =VLOOKUP(E2, Bands!$A$2:$B$4, 2, TRUE).
A two-way lookup uses two MATCHes: =INDEX(grid, MATCH(row_label, row_labels, 0), MATCH(column_label, column_labels, 0)) picks one cell from a table by its row and column headings.

lessons.title: When lookups fail
objectives: Diagnose #N/A and wrong results from lookups
Choose between IFNA and IFERROR
Check that every key found a match
key_points: #N/A means no match: often a trailing space ('BR01 '), a number stored as text (101 against "101"), a different spelling, or a code that's genuinely missing from the lookup table; lookups ignore case, so capitals alone aren't the problem.
IFNA(formula, "Not found") replaces only #N/A, while IFERROR replaces every error, including a misspelt range or a #DIV/0!, so prefer IFNA (or XLOOKUP's if_not_found) to avoid hiding real mistakes.
Count the failures rather than scrolling for them: =COUNTIF(K:K, "Not found") gives how many rows found nothing, and a filter on the column shows which codes they were.
If the lookup table has a duplicate key, every lookup quietly returns the first match, so check that keys are unique, with COUNTIF, before relying on it.
Decide what a missing match means for totals: rows marked Not found have no cost, so their profit is left blank rather than zero, and a report should say how many sales that leaves out.

The starter file products.csv: 16 products with their code, name, category and unit cost
XLOOKUP needs Microsoft 365 or Excel 2021 or later, Google Sheets, or LibreOffice Calc 24.8 or later; otherwise use the INDEX/MATCH and VLOOKUP versions given in each step

steps.do: Import products.csv into a new sheet called Products (A1:D17). Add a sheet called Bands with these values in A1:B4, smallest threshold first.

In J2 and K2, look up the product's name and category, with Not found when the code isn't listed.

J2: =XLOOKUP(D2,Products!$A$2:$A$17,Products!$B$2:$B$17,"Not found")

modules.title: Conditional aggregates, pivot tables and charts
modules.summary: Summarise sales with SUMIFS, COUNTIFS and AVERAGEIFS, build a branch-by-month grid with one formula, check it with a pivot table, and chart the result.

lessons.title: SUMIFS, COUNTIFS and AVERAGEIFS
objectives: Sum, count and average with conditions
Write criteria with operators, cell references, dates and wildcards
Build a summary grid with one formula
key_points: SUMIFS(sum_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, ...) adds the values whose rows meet every condition, as in =SUMIFS(Sales!H:H, Sales!C:C, "Central", Sales!O:O, 3) for Central's March revenue; COUNTIFS and AVERAGEIFS work the same way, and MAXIFS and MINIFS return the extremes.
The older SUMIF takes the range to add last, but SUMIFS takes it first; in both, every range must be the same size, or the formula returns an error.

Criteria are written as text: ">=10" for a comparison, "<>Cash" for 'not', ">="&H1 to compare with a cell, ">="&DATE(2025,10,1) for dates, and the wildcards * (any characters) and ? (one character), as in "BR*".
Several conditions in one SUMIFS mean AND; for OR, add two SUMIFS together, such as card payments plus mobile payments.

One formula fills a whole grid when its references are mixed: with branch names in column A ($A2) and month numbers in row 1 (B$1), =SUMIFS(Sales!$H:$H, Sales!$C:$C, $A2, Sales!$O:$O, B$1) can be copied across and down.
Check a summary against its source: the grid's grand total should equal =SUM(Sales!H:H), and a difference means some rows matched no label, such as a misspelt branch.

lessons.title: Pivot tables
objectives: Summarise data with a pivot table
Group dates by month and show values as a share of the total
Keep a pivot table up to date
key_points: A pivot table summarises a table without formulas: choose fields for its rows (branch), columns (month) and values (sum of revenue), and optionally filters, and it totals every combination.

Create one from a tidy table with Insert > PivotTable in Excel, Insert > Pivot table in Google Sheets or Insert > Pivot Table in LibreOffice Calc, then drag or add fields to rows, columns, values and filters.
Values can be summed, counted or averaged, and shown as a share of the grand total: Show Values As in Excel, Show as in Google Sheets, and the displayed value option in Calc's data field settings.
Dates can be grouped by month, quarter or year: right-click a date and choose Group in Excel or Create pivot date group in Google Sheets, or use Data > Group and Outline > Group in LibreOffice Calc.
Excel and Calc pivot tables don't update by themselves when the data changes: refresh them (right-click > Refresh); Google Sheets pivot tables update automatically.
Pivot tables and SUMIFS grids answer the same questions: a pivot table is quicker to build and change, while formulas keep a fixed layout that other formulas and charts can rely on.

walkthrough.tool: Excel, Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc
walkthrough.title: Build a pivot table of revenue by branch and month

steps.do: Click any cell in the Sales sheet's data.
steps.see: All three apps detect the whole table around the cell.

steps.do: Excel: choose Insert > PivotTable, keep the suggested range, choose New Worksheet and OK. Drag branch to Rows, month to Columns and revenue to Values.
Google Sheets: choose Insert > Pivot table, choose New sheet and Create. In the pivot table editor, add branch under Rows, month under Columns and revenue under Values, summarised by SUM.
LibreOffice Calc: choose Insert > Pivot Table, keep Current selection and OK. Drag branch to Row Fields, month to Column Fields and revenue to Data Fields (it shows Sum - revenue), then OK.
steps.see: The pivot table appears on a new sheet.

steps.do: Compare the grand total with Totals!B4: both should be 4,017.50.

Show the values as shares: in Excel right-click a value and choose Show Values As > % of Grand Total; in Google Sheets set Show as to % of grand total; in Calc double-click the data field and choose a displayed value of % of total.
Try grouping real dates: put date instead of month in the columns, then group it by months (Group in Excel, Create pivot date group in Google Sheets, Data > Group and Outline > Group in Calc).

lessons.title: Charts from summaries
objectives: Choose a chart type for a summary
Create and tidy a chart in Excel, Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc
Add sparklines beside a table
key_points: Chart a summary, not raw rows: a column chart of revenue by branch from three totals, or a line chart of revenue by month from twelve, reads far better than a chart of 368 sales.

Create a chart by selecting the summary, labels included, and choosing Insert > Chart (Excel's Recommended Charts suggests types), then edit titles, axes and series in the chart editor or the format pane.
Use bars or columns for categories and lines for months, and avoid 3-D effects and pies with many slices; a bar's axis must start at zero, so check the axis minimum if the app chose another.

Title the chart with what it shows, such as 'November was the busiest month', label axes with their units, and remove legends and gridlines that add nothing; Data Storytelling and Dashboard Design goes further.
Sparklines are tiny charts inside cells, one per row of a table: Insert > Sparklines in Excel, =SPARKLINE(B2:M2) in Google Sheets, and Insert > Sparkline in LibreOffice Calc 7.4 or later.
A chart made from a pivot table (a PivotChart in Excel) follows the pivot table, changing when it's filtered or refreshed.

lab.title: Summarise sales by branch and month
lab.tool: Excel, Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc
lab.goal: Build a branch-by-month revenue grid from one SUMIFS formula, answer the owners' questions with COUNTIFS, AVERAGEIFS, MAXIFS and date criteria, check the grid against a pivot table, and chart the monthly totals.
setup: Your course workbook, with the Sales sheet's revenue, category and profit columns from the earlier labs

steps.do: On Sales, type month in O1 and the sale's month number in O2; fill it down to row 369.
steps.see: 1 for the first sale.

steps.do: Add a sheet called Summary. Type branch in A1, the numbers 1 to 12 in B1:M1 and Total in N1; in A2:A4 type Central, Market and Station, and in A5 Total.
In B2, write one formula with mixed references, then fill it across to M2 and down to row 4.
steps.see: Central's January revenue in B2.

steps.do: Add the totals: =SUM(B2:M2) in N2 (filled down to N4), and =SUM(B2:B4) in B5 (filled across to N5). Format the grid with two decimal places.
steps.see: N5 is 4,017.50, the same as Totals!B4.

steps.do: Below the grid, answer the owners' questions in A7:B13.
steps.code:
A7  Card share of revenue          B7  =SUMIFS(Sales!H:H,Sales!G:G,"Card")/SUM(Sales!H:H)
A8  Card sales lines               B8  =COUNTIFS(Sales!G:G,"Card")
A9  Average pastry quantity        B9  =AVERAGEIFS(Sales!E:E,Sales!K:K,"Pastry")
A10 Largest Market sale            B10 =MAXIFS(Sales!H:H,Sales!C:C,"Market")

The grid's grand total matches the Sales sheet.
The card share and the October to December revenue are right.
The average pastry quantity and cakes profit are right.

lab.submit: Paste the Summary sheet's grid (A1:N5) and A7:B13, and describe your chart's title and type in a sentence.
hints: A grid of zeros usually means month numbers in row 1 are text: type them as numbers, or check column O holds numbers.
If the October to December revenue is 0 but the grid is right, the dates in column B were imported as text: re-import with date detection on, or use the month column instead.
An error from SUMIFS (#VALUE! in Excel) often means its ranges are different sizes: whole columns (H:H, C:C) avoid that.
MAXIFS needs Excel 2019 or later, Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc 5.2 or later.

modules.title: Data validation and what-if analysis
modules.summary: Stop bad input with data validation, build a model that separates assumptions from calculations, compare scenarios and use Goal Seek, then check and document a workbook before sharing it.

lessons.title: Data validation
objectives: Restrict input with drop-down lists and number and date rules
Write helpful input messages and error alerts
Find invalid data that's already in a sheet
key_points: Data validation limits what can be entered in cells: a drop-down list from a range (such as the branch names), whole or decimal numbers between limits, dates in a range, or text of a set length (Data > Data Validation in Excel, Data > Data validation in Google Sheets, Data > Validity in LibreOffice Calc).
An input message tells people what to enter when they select the cell, and the error alert decides what happens to bad input: reject it, or warn and allow it.
Excel and Google Sheets also accept a custom formula rule, such as =COUNTIF($A:$A, A2)=1 to stop a sale ID being entered twice.

Validation checks new entries, not what was already there or pasted over it, so look for existing problems: Data Validation > Circle Invalid Data in Excel, Tools > Detective > Mark Invalid Data in LibreOffice Calc, and the red marker Google Sheets shows on invalid cells.

Protect formulas from accidental edits by protecting the sheet and leaving only the input cells unlocked: Review > Protect Sheet in Excel, Tools > Protect Sheet in LibreOffice Calc, and Data > Protect sheets and ranges in Google Sheets.

lessons.title: What-if analysis
objectives: Separate a model's inputs from its calculations
Compare scenarios with a table of input values
Find the input that reaches a target with Goal Seek
key_points: A model keeps its inputs (assumptions such as price, cost and units sold) in clearly labelled, coloured cells, and every calculation refers to them, so changing one input updates every result.

A scenario table lists several values of one input down a column, with the result's formula beside each, such as profit at price changes from -10% to +10%; Excel's Data Table and Calc's Data > Multiple Operations build such a table from one formula, and in Google Sheets you write the formulas yourself.

Goal Seek finds the input value that makes a formula reach a target: Data > What-If Analysis > Goal Seek in Excel (Set cell, To value, By changing cell) and Tools > Goal Seek in LibreOffice Calc; Google Sheets needs a Goal Seek add-on.

Goal Seek adjusts one input step by step until the result is close enough; when two inputs give the target, such as a small or a large price rise, it finds the one nearest its starting value, so try more than one start.
Scenario Manager in Excel and Tools > Scenarios in LibreOffice Calc store named sets of inputs, such as best, expected and worst case, so they can be switched and compared.

A model is only as good as its assumptions: write each one down with where it came from, such as 'each 1% price rise loses 1.2% of sales, the owners' estimate', and test how much the answer changes if it's wrong.

walkthrough.title: Find a target with Goal Seek

steps.do: Open the Model sheet from the module 5 lab, set the price change in B5 to 0 and check that the profit in B12 is 620.00.
Excel: choose Data > What-If Analysis > Goal Seek. Set cell B12, To value 700, By changing cell B4, then OK.
steps.see: B4 becomes 45.16 units a month, and B12 shows 700.00.

steps.do: LibreOffice Calc: choose Tools > Goal Seek. Formula cell B12, Target value 700, Variable cell B4, then OK and Yes to keep the result.
steps.see: The same answer: 45.16.

steps.do: Put B4 back to 40, then goal-seek B12 to 625 by changing B5, starting from 0.
steps.see: B5 becomes about 0.027: a 2.7% price rise.

steps.do: Now set B5 to 0.15 and goal-seek again to 625.
steps.see: About 0.160: a 16.0% rise reaches the same profit, because fewer cakes are sold; Goal Seek finds the answer nearest its start.

steps.do: Set B5 back to 0.05 for the lab's later steps.

lessons.title: Checking and sharing a workbook
objectives: Audit formulas with precedents and dependents
Reconcile totals and document a workbook
Share files in a form that works for their readers
key_points: Trace precedents and dependents to see which cells feed a formula and which rely on it (Formulas > Trace Precedents in Excel, Tools > Detective in LibreOffice Calc); in Google Sheets, clicking into a formula outlines the ranges it uses.
Reconcile totals worked out two ways: the summary grid's grand total and =SUM(Sales!H:H) should agree, and a check cell holding their difference should show zero.
Add a README sheet with the workbook's purpose, its data sources and dates, what each sheet holds, the assumptions and who to ask, so others (and you, later) can trust it.

Functions differ between apps and versions: XLOOKUP, UNIQUE and FILTER don't exist in older Excel or older LibreOffice and show #NAME? there, so check what your readers use, or share the results as values or a PDF.

Excel's .xlsx, LibreOffice's .ods and Google Sheets open each other's files, but macros, some pivot table settings and chart formatting may change on the way, so open the file in your reader's app before sending it.

Use version history instead of copies called final_v2: File > Version history in Google Sheets, version history for Excel files saved to OneDrive or SharePoint, and File > Versions in LibreOffice Calc.

lab.title: Build a price-change model
lab.tool: Excel, Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc
lab.goal: Build a what-if model for the bakery's celebration cakes: inputs in validated cells, outputs that follow them, a scenario table of price changes, and Goal Seek answers to the owners' two questions.
setup: The owners' estimates: celebration cakes sell for 24.00, cost 8.50 to make, and sell 40 a month; they think each 1% price rise would lose 1.2% of sales
For Goal Seek: Excel or LibreOffice Calc, or the Goal Seek add-on in Google Sheets

steps.do: Add a sheet called Model and type the inputs in A1:B6; give B2:B6 a fill colour so everyone can see they're inputs.
steps.code:
A1 Inputs
A2 Price (£)                                     B2 24
A3 Unit cost (£)                                 B3 8.5
A4 Units a month                                  B4 40
A5 Price change                                  B5 5%
A6 Change in units for each 1% price rise (%)   B6 -1.2

steps.do: Type the outputs in A8:B12, each referring only to the inputs.
steps.code:
A8 Outputs
A9  New price   B9  =B2*(1+B5)
A10 New units   B10 =B4*(1+B6*B5)
A11 Revenue     B11 =B9*B10
A12 Profit      B12 =(B9-B3)*B10

steps.do: Build a scenario table: Price change in D1 and Profit in E1, the changes -10%, -5%, 0%, 5% and 10% in D2:D6, and this formula in E2, filled down to E6.

Validate the inputs: B5 must be a decimal between -0.5 and 0.5, and B6 between -5 and 0. Add an input message to each and set the error alert to reject bad values (Data > Data Validation in Excel, Data > Data validation in Google Sheets, Data > Validity in LibreOffice Calc).
Test the rule: type 80% in B5.
steps.see: The entry is rejected with your error message.

steps.do: Answer the owners' first question with Goal Seek, as lesson 2's walkthrough shows: how many cakes a month would make 700.00 profit at today's price? Set B5 to 0 first, and put B4 back to 40 afterwards.
steps.see: 45.16 cakes a month.

steps.do: Answer the second: what price rise would make 625.00 profit? Goal-seek B12 to 625 by changing B5, first from 0 and then from 15%, and note both answers. Then set B5 back to 5%.
steps.see: 2.7% from 0, and 16.0% from 15%.

steps.do: Add a README sheet: the workbook's purpose, the data sources, each sheet's job, the model's assumptions and their source, and the date.

checks.text: The model's outputs for a 5% price rise are right.
The scenario table is right at both ends.
Goal Seek finds the cakes a month needed for a profit of 700.00.
Goal Seek finds both price rises that give a profit of 625.00.

lab.submit: Paste A1:B12 and D1:E6 from the Model sheet, your two Goal Seek answers with their starting values, and your README sheet's text.
hints: If New units doesn't change with the price, check that B10 multiplies B6 by B5: the units change depends on the price change.
Type percentages with the % sign (5%) or as decimals (0.05); 5 on its own means 500%.
If Goal Seek reports it can't find a solution, check the target is reachable: no price change gives a profit above about 630 with these assumptions.
Goal Seek's answers are approximate, so 0.0270 or 0.0271 are both right; format B5 as a percentage with one decimal.

study_plan.focus: Tidy data, importing CSV files, formulas and references; build the sales totals in the lab.
Clean text, dates and numbers stored as text, and find duplicates; clean the online orders.
XLOOKUP, INDEX/MATCH and VLOOKUP, and lookups that fail; add product details and profit.
SUMIFS, COUNTIFS, pivot tables and charts; summarise sales by branch and month.
Data validation, what-if analysis and Goal Seek; build the price-change model.
Build the capstone workbook and summary for the owners, then review with the mock exam and the flashcards.

project.title: Analyse a year of sales for the bakery's owners
project.brief: Morning Loaf's owners want one workbook that answers their questions about 2025 and helps them plan 2026. Using sales_2025.csv, products.csv and online_orders.csv, build it in Excel, Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc. It needs: the sales data, untouched, on its own sheet, with revenue, fees, product details and profit added by formulas; the online orders cleaned, with duplicates flagged and a cleaning log; a summary sheet answering, with SUMIFS-style formulas, which branch, category and month earn the most revenue and gross profit, how customers pay, and what the unlisted seasonal specials added; a pivot table that reconciles with the formulas; at least three charts titled with their findings; a validated what-if model for a price change in the category you'd recommend changing, with a scenario table and a Goal Seek answer; and a README sheet. Finish with a one-page summary for the owners: five findings with their numbers, one recommendation, and the limits of the data (a sample of 30 sales lines a month, and unit costs covering ingredients only).
deliverables: The workbook: raw data, calculated columns, cleaned online orders, summary, pivot table, charts, model and README sheets
A reconciliation: the pivot table's and the formulas' grand totals side by side, with their difference
At least three charts, each titled with its finding
The what-if model, with validated inputs, a scenario table and a Goal Seek answer
A one-page summary for the owners: five findings with numbers, a recommendation and the data's limits

rubric.name: Data set-up and cleaning
rubric.description: Raw data kept separate and tidy; the online orders cleaned with formulas, duplicates flagged and a cleaning log kept.

rubric.name: Formulas and lookups
rubric.description: Calculated columns use correct relative, absolute and mixed references; lookups handle missing codes clearly and their ranges are locked.

rubric.name: Summaries
rubric.description: SUMIFS, COUNTIFS and AVERAGEIFS answers are right, a pivot table reconciles with them, and the grand totals agree.

rubric.name: Charts
rubric.description: Suitable chart types made from summaries, titled with their findings, with labelled axes starting at zero for bars.

rubric.name: What-if model
rubric.description: Inputs separated, labelled and validated; outputs follow them; a scenario table and a correctly used Goal Seek.

rubric.name: Findings and documentation
rubric.description: A README that explains the workbook, and a summary whose findings are correct, specific and honest about the data's limits.

project.submit: Paste or link your workbook (a shared Google Sheets link, or the file), your reconciliation, and your one-page summary for the owners.
